conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; atr(n) is the n-bar average true range

candidates.name: FailedSignalReversalEntry
candidates.quote: The most common example of a morphed pattern is a failure, where a pattern fails to yield a scalper's profit and then reverses into a signal in the other direction.
candidates.description: Meta-rule: any entry signal that fails to reach a scalper's profit within a bounded number of bars, followed by price breaking beyond that signal bar's opposite extreme with a reversal-quality bar, becomes a new entry signal in the opposite direction.
candidates.pseudocode: signalFailed(bar S) = withinFailBars(S) && never reached scalpTicks favorable move from S's trigger price; reverse when close[0] crosses beyond S's opposite extreme with a reversal bar
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (meta-pattern; enters as a stop beyond the new reversal bar)

complexity.reason: 'pattern' and 'signal' are unspecified here -- which setups count as a trackable signal, and how 'failed to reach a scalper's profit' is measured for a signal that was never actually filled, is a design decision before this can be coded at all

notes: Generalizes the second-entry idea (Chapter 10's SecondReversalSignal) and the failed-breakout family to ANY signal, not just reversal bars.
A narrower, codable version: only track the engine's own last Entry signal per placement (its trigger price and bar index) rather than every chart pattern.

candidates.name: IgnoreStaleFailedSignal
candidates.quote: If the failure just goes sideways for a number of bars and then a new pattern develops, it makes more sense to simply regard the new pattern as being independent of the first.
candidates.description: Caps T12-01: only treat a new signal as a failure-reversal of a prior one if it triggers within maxBarsAfterFailure bars of the failure; beyond that, evaluate it independently (i.e., T12-01 does not fire).

complexity.reason: needs a persisted bars-since counter keyed to the prior failed signal

candidates.name: LargeGapOpenFavorsTrendDay
candidates.quote: Large gap openings often lead to trend days in either direction.
candidates.description: Intraday filter: when the session's opening gap (open minus the prior session's close) exceeds a multiple of ATR, bias toward with-trend entries and treat the day as a likely trend day rather than a trading-range day.

complexity.reason: single session-open-vs-prior-close comparison against ATR; deciding which direction is 'the trend' is left to other filters

candidates.name: OpposingSpikesPredictTradingRange
candidates.quote: The market had bull spikes up to bar 2 and bar 4 and bear spikes down to bar 3 and bar 5. This often results in a trading range as the bulls and bears continue to trade in an attempt to generate a channel in their direction.
candidates.description: Filter: when two or more opposing-direction spikes (runs of spikeBars consecutive trend bars) have alternated within the last windowBars, treat the market as entering a trading range rather than a trend and prefer fading extremes over trend-following.

complexity.reason: needs a spike-detection primitive plus counting direction changes among detected spikes over a variable window

candidates.name: FirstHourDoubleTopToDoubleBottomBothEntries
candidates.quote: In the first hour, double top bear flags often evolve into double bottom bull flags and vice versa... you should look to take both entries... because a big move is common from either the first or second of these patterns.
candidates.description: Intraday: within the first hour, take the short below a double top and, if it fails, the long above the subsequent double bottom formed near the same swing low(s).
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop below the double top / buy stop above the double bottom (mechanized: next bar open)

complexity.reason: needs a DoubleTop/DoubleBottom pivot-tolerance pattern definition (book 3 territory) plus a first-hour session gate; no such primitive exists yet in this chapter

rejected.quote: Names are never important. Just make sure that you read correctly what is in front of you and place your trade, ignoring the pattern that completed a couple of bars earlier.
An expanding triangle sometimes expands from five legs to seven.
rejected.reason: descriptive fact about an existing pattern's leg count, not an independent bar-level test.

rejected.quote: If you are aggressively trading the market in question, you should look to take both entries, and swing part of them
rejected.reason: position sizing / scaling, not a bar condition; the engine trades fixed size.

rejected.quote: A bull spike and channel trend pattern usually evolves into a trading range and then a double bottom bull flag.
rejected.reason: multi-stage statistical narrative chaining three undefined chart patterns; no single decidable test beyond the alternating-spike proxy already captured in T12-04.

chapter_summary: Chapter 12 is mostly worked chart examples showing how one setup morphs into another, especially failures that reverse into opposite-direction signals. It produced one high-value but research-grade meta-rule (a failed signal becomes an opposite signal, T12-01/02), plus three narrower, more codable context filters drawn from the two figures: a large opening gap favoring a trend day, alternating opposing spikes favoring a trading range, and a first-hour double-top-to-double-bottom both-entries idea. Most of the chapter's pattern-naming ('wedge bull flag', 'spike and channel', 'high 2'/'low 2') reuses primitives defined in Chapters 10, 15, 18-21 and produced no new candidates here.
